walkthroughs.body_html:
P = I × V and P = I² × R ⚡

Both give power in watts. Use IV when you know current and voltage; use I²R when you know current and resistance.

They're linked through Ohm's law: V = IR. If you sub V = IR into P = IV, you get P = I²R.

Every wire has some resistance. As current flows, P = I²R is dissipated as heat.

Doubling the current makes the heating four times bigger — that's why high-current appliances need thick cables.

Cables that overheat are a fire risk. Fuses break the circuit before that happens.

Pick the smallest standard fuse above the appliance's normal current. UK fuses are usually 3 A, 5 A or 13 A.

Example: a 230 V, 1000 W heater draws I = P ÷ V = 1000 ÷ 230 ≈ 4.3 A. A 5 A fuse is the right choice.

A fuse that's too big won't blow when it should. Too small and it blows during normal use.

options: P = V ÷ I
P = I² × R
P = R ÷ I²
P = I × R

options: 1 A
3 A

mcqs.q: What is the difference between energy and power?
options: Power is the energy used over the lifetime of a device.
Voltage measures how many electrons are stored in a battery.
Energy is measured in joules; power is the rate of energy transfer, measured in watts (joules per second).
Energy and power are the same — both describe how much fuel something uses.

mcqs.q: What happens to the current as it goes around a series circuit?
options: Power is the energy used over the lifetime of a device.
Current gets used up by each component as it flows around the circuit.
It stays the same at every point — current is conserved.
Current splits in half at the battery so each direction gets some.

mcqs.q: What does voltage (potential difference) across a component represent?
options: Power is the energy used over the lifetime of a device.
Voltage measures how many electrons are stored in a battery.
The energy transferred per unit charge passing through that component.
Voltage is the 'amount of electricity' flowing through the wire.
